title: Design exercise: file storage and sync
summary: A classic design exercise: a folder-sync service at hundreds of petabytes with version history, sharing and resumable uploads. The reference answer splits files into content-addressed 4 MB blocks, keeps a strongly consistent metadata namespace per account, runs a commit protocol that reports missing blocks, stores hot blocks replicated and cold blocks erasure coded, and treats repair time, soft deletion and restore tests as part of durability.

exercise.prompt: Design a file storage and sync service: users install a client that keeps a folder in sync across their devices and the web, share folders with other users, and can recover earlier versions of a file. Uploads must survive flaky connections and the service must never lose a file it has acknowledged.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Upload, download and delete files and folders; sync changes to every device of the account within seconds; version history for 30 days (assumption).
Share a folder with other accounts; resumable uploads; web access.
50 million users, 10 million active per day; an average of 5 GB stored per user, so 250 PB of logical data.
100 million file changes per day with an average file of 1 MB; 30 percent of uploaded bytes are duplicates of blocks already stored (assumption).
derive the ingest rate, the physical storage per durability scheme and the metadata volume yourself
Durability designed so that losing a file requires several simultaneous disk or node failures, with a stated repair time; 99.9 percent availability for sync.
A change visible on other devices within 10 s at p95; a 1 MB file uploads in under 2 s at p95 on a good connection.
Collaborative editing of file contents, search inside files, virus scanning, end-to-end encryption (server-side encryption at rest is assumed).

clarifying_questions.q: What is the unit of storage?
clarifying_questions.a: A block: files are split into fixed-size blocks of up to 4 MB, each named by its content hash, so identical blocks are stored once. Dropbox's public description of Magic Pocket uses exactly this unit.

clarifying_questions.q: What happens when two devices edit the same file offline?
clarifying_questions.a: The second commit sees a version mismatch and the client saves a conflicted copy beside the original; nothing is merged and nothing is lost.

clarifying_questions.q: Is the file namespace strongly consistent?
clarifying_questions.a: Yes, per account: a rename or a delete is linearizable within the account's metadata shard. Cross-account sharing is eventually consistent (seconds).

clarifying_questions.q: How long are deleted files kept?
clarifying_questions.a: 30 days in a soft-deleted state, then blocks are unreferenced and garbage collected (assumption).
Most bytes are written once and rarely read; most reads are of recent files. Storage is tiered by age and access.
Metadata lives in one region per account; blocks are replicated across regions for disaster survival. The reference answer stays single-region for the request paths.

blocks.text: Erasure coding of cold data is what both Dropbox's Magic Pocket write-up and the S3 write-up describe, each with its own parameters. Hot data stays replicated because a replicated block is read from one disk, while an erasure-coded block needs several fragments reassembled.

The client does the hard work: it splits files into blocks, hashes them, and computes which blocks the server lacks. The metadata service owns the namespace (files, folders, versions, block lists, sharing) in a strongly consistent store sharded by account. The block service stores immutable, content-addressed blocks in a hot replicated tier and a cold erasure-coded tier, with repair and tiering workers behind it. A change feed per account drives a notification service that tells other devices to sync.

Metadata and blocks are separate systems with separate consistency rules: the frame is the metadata system, and the boxes below it are the block system. The notification arrow is a hint: the cursor fetch guarantees completeness.

blocks.text: The Google File System paper is the ancestor of this split: a single master holding the metadata, chunkservers holding large chunks (64 MB in the paper), and three replicas by default. Dropbox's Magic Pocket describes the modern form the answer follows: blocks of up to 4 MB named by their hash, replicated for durability and erasure coded once cold.

blocks.legend: The write half of the architecture, the neutral diagram's boxes with one AWS service each: the metadata service and the block service are ECS on Fargate tasks behind the load balancer, and the neutral sharing box is the metadata service's sharing routes, so it has no box of its own; the metadata DB is a DynamoDB table with one partition key per account, whose commit is one transaction s12; the change feed is items of that same table, written in the commit's transaction; the blocks are S3 objects named by their hash, hot in S3 Standard and cold in Glacier Instant Retrieval, which keep millisecond access s23. The client uploads each block straight to S3 with a URL the block service signed s21, so no block passes through a task; where the neutral API has PUT and GET /blocks/{hash} and GET /notify, this section has POST /blocks/urls and /blocks/done, presigned PUT and GET calls to S3, and a WebSocket; the neutral Cursor is the cursor the client holds and sends, and Account quota, rename, restore and share revocation are plain items of the same table that this pass does not draw. The repair and tiering workers have no box of their own: S3 repairs its own storage across a minimum of three Availability Zones s24, and the tiering is a lifecycle rule s25; what remains of the neutral workers is the garbage collector, shown at the bottom as one Lambda box that stands for two functions: the stream function that counts references, and the hourly sweep. The write half carries them so that the read half stays within 12 nodes; the stream has at most two functions, the other being the notification function, which also copies commits to a shared folder into each member's feed s18. The blocks table is the one box the neutral diagram leaves implicit. Sync means the caller waits for the answer; async means the work goes on after the caller has been answered. The load balancer sits in the public subnets of one VPC and every task in its private subnets, across three Availability Zones in one Region.

blocks.legend: The read half: the neutral diagram's sync path, one AWS service each. A device fetches the changes after its cursor from the metadata service, which queries the feed items of its account with a strongly consistent read s14. To download, the device names the version and the hashes it lacks; the metadata service, which owns the permission check (the neutral sharing and permissions box), reads the version item and, when the folder is not the caller's, the share item, and only then signs a download URL with its task role s21, so a hash alone is never enough to read a block; the device then downloads straight from S3, and the block service is not in the read half. The notification service is an API Gateway WebSocket API whose backend is a Lambda function: a Lambda authorizer on the $connect route checks the device's token (the only route on which API Gateway allows an authorizer) s47, the function then stores the connection id with the device's account s43 and removes it on $disconnect; DynamoDB Streams records each commit's feed item for 24 hours s17, the function reads the stream through an event source mapping s18, looks up the account's connections and posts a hint to each over the WebSocket s29. The hint carries no data; the cursor fetch does. The devices appear twice, once calling the API and once holding the WebSocket; they are the same devices. Waking a sleeping phone is the extension that the notification decision names; it is not drawn. Sync means the caller waits for the answer; async means the work goes on after the caller has moved on. The connections table is the one box the neutral diagram leaves implicit.

  Edge->>MS: HTTP, a healthy task

blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed. Edge is the Application Load Balancer, which routes only to healthy targets s6; ECS replaces a failed task s7. The node read is strongly consistent, so the version check sees the latest commit s14. A 412 sends the client to save a conflicted copy. The calls to DynamoDB go over a gateway endpoint s10.

blocks.text: The metadata service never touches block bytes: it reads one node and asks the blocks table which hashes exist. If either check fails, the client gets its answer before anything is written.
Part b: the upload, straight from the client to S3.

sequenceDiagram autonumber 11 participant C as Client participant Edge as Load balancer participant BS as Block svc participant S3 as S3 participant DDB as DynamoDB C->>Edge: POST /blocks/urls, hashes Edge->>BS: HTTP BS-->>Edge: one presigned PUT per hash Edge-->>C: the URLs Note over BS: signed with the task role,
SHA-256 of the block bound loop each missing block C->>S3: PUT the block, presigned URL opt the connection drops mid-PUT C->>S3: PUT the same block again end S3-->>C: 200, checksum verified end C->>Edge: POST /blocks/done, hashes Edge->>BS: HTTP BS->>S3: HeadObject per hash S3-->>BS: the sizes BS->>DDB: PutItem, if the hash is new Note over BS,DDB: count 0, zero_since now,
a failed condition counts as done BS-->>Edge: 200 Edge-->>C: 200
blocks.legend: The block service signs each URL with its own task role, and the URL carries that role's permissions and an expiry s21; a SHA-256 supplied with the upload is checked by S3 against the body s22. A PUT that S3 acknowledges is stored across at least three Availability Zones s24, which is the neutral rule that a block is replicated before it is acknowledged. If two clients race on the same hash, the second PUT replaces the first with identical bytes, which is harmless. Block bytes never pass through a task; the HeadObject confirms the object before the table says it exists. The PutItem on the blocks table carries a condition that the hash does not exist s44: if two clients uploaded the same new block, the second PutItem fails the condition and counts as done, so it can never reset the count of a block that a version already references.

blocks.text: Nothing in this part changes a version: an upload that never reaches the second commit leaves a block with a zero reference count, which the sweep removes after two days.
Part c: the second commit, one transaction.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 25 participant C as Client participant Edge as Load balancer participant MS as Metadata svc participant DDB as DynamoDB C->>Edge: POST /commit, same list Edge->>MS: HTTP MS->>DDB: GetItem, the account's sequence number DDB-->>MS: N, strongly consistent MS->>DDB: TransactWriteItems Note over MS,DDB: conditions on the parent version
and on the sequence number N, then
put version, update node, put feed item
with N+1, set the TTL of the superseded version alt the transaction commits DDB-->>MS: durable MS-->>Edge: 200, the version Edge-->>C: 200, the version else the parent version moved DDB-->>MS: canceled, the version condition MS-->>Edge: 412 Edge-->>C: 412, save a conflicted copy else the sequence moved DDB-->>MS: canceled, the sequence condition Note over MS: another commit of the account got N first:
read the number again and retry end
blocks.legend: One transaction carries every item of the commit, five actions, one of them the update that gives the version this commit supersedes a TTL of 30 days, so only noncurrent versions ever expire and the current version of an untouched file never does (a delete does the same for the current version, 30 days after the soft delete); all actions succeed or none does s12, and DynamoDB writes each item twice underneath, one to prepare and one to commit s13. The service reads the sequence item first, because an update inside a transaction returns no value, and conditions the transaction on it; the condition is what makes the feed a log with a monotonic sequence: two commits racing on one account cannot take the same number. A cancelled transaction names the condition that failed, item by item s46: only a failed parent-version condition is a real conflict and becomes the 412, while a failed sequence condition means a commit of another file got the number first, so the service reads the number again and retries, and the client never sees it. All of an account's items share one partition key, so a very busy account is where the limit of 1,000 write units a second that a partition delivers would show first s15; the namespace split by folder subtree in the 10x section is the remedy.

blocks.text: Sharing, the second write path of the neutral design: the metadata service's sharing routes write the membership and one feed item into every member's partition.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 37 participant Own as Owner participant Edge as Load balancer participant MS as Metadata svc participant DDB as DynamoDB Own->>Edge: POST /shares, folder, member, role Edge->>MS: HTTP, a healthy task MS->>DDB: transaction in the owner's partition Note over MS,DDB: the share item, the sequence
condition, a feed item DDB-->>MS: durable loop each member MS->>DDB: transaction in the member's partition Note over MS,DDB: a marker item (once only),
the sequence condition, a feed item DDB-->>MS: durable end alt every member is done MS-->>Edge: 200 Edge-->>Own: 200 else a member's transaction failed MS-->>Edge: 503, the client repeats the call Edge-->>Own: 503 end
blocks.legend: Sharing is the same commit pattern with a different payload: the membership is written in the owner's partition, and each member gets a feed item in their own partition through one transaction that increments that member's sequence under a condition s12, so a member's feed stays a log with a monotonic sequence whoever writes to it. No transaction crosses accounts, which keeps sharing eventual on purpose, as in the neutral design. The marker item, written once with a condition that it does not exist s44, makes a repeated call after a failure a no-op for the members already done.

blocks.text: A member whose transaction fails makes the whole call return 503; the client repeats it, and the members already done are skipped by their marker items, so a share is complete when the call finally returns 200. Later commits to a shared folder reach each member's feed through the notification function (see the read path), so a member sees the owner's edits and not only the share.
The read path through AWS, part a: how a device learns that something changed.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 47
  participant Dev as Device
  participant WS as WebSocket API
  participant Auth as Authorizer fn
  participant Fn as Notification fn
  participant DDB as DynamoDB
  Dev->>WS: connect, with its token
  WS->>Auth: the $connect authorizer
  Auth-->>WS: allow, with the account id
  WS->>Fn: the $connect route
  Fn->>DDB: PutItem, connection id and account
  WS-->>Dev: connected
  Note over DDB: a commit wrote a feed item
  DDB-)Fn: stream record
  opt a commit to a shared folder
    Fn->>DDB: transaction in each member's partition
  end
  Fn->>DDB: Query the connections table
  DDB-->>Fn: connection ids of the account
  Fn->>WS: PostToConnection, account and sequence
  WS-)Dev: a hint over the WebSocket
  opt the connection is gone
    WS-->>Fn: 410 Gone
    Fn->>DDB: delete the connection id
  end
  opt the device disconnects
    WS->>Fn: the $disconnect route
    Fn->>DDB: delete the connection id
  end
blocks.legend: The device registers when it connects: the $connect route is the one place API Gateway allows an authorizer, and a Lambda authorizer there can check a token and pass on the account id s47; only after it allows the connection does the route's function store the connection id with the account s43. The token comes from the sign-in of the product, which is outside this lesson. The same function handles $disconnect and the stream. For a commit to a shared folder it also writes the change into each member's feed, in one transaction per member like the share call; each such insert reaches the same function through the stream, so the members' devices are notified by the same path. The open arrows are hand-offs: the stream record reaches the function through the event source mapping, and the hint reaches the device whenever the connection is up. A WebSocket connection lasts at most 2 hours and is dropped after 10 idle minutes s28, so a device reconnects and fetches by cursor; the hint is an optimisation and the cursor fetch is the guarantee. The stream keeps records for 24 hours s17. The function posts through the connection commands of the API s29.

blocks.text: The hint can be late, lost or duplicated without harm, because the device always asks by cursor; the stream and the WebSocket only shorten the wait.
Part b: the cursor fetch and the download of the one block the device lacks.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 63
  participant Dev as Device
  participant Edge as Load balancer
  participant MS as Metadata svc
  participant DDB as DynamoDB
  participant S3 as S3
  Dev->>Edge: GET /changes?cursor=
  Edge->>MS: HTTP
  MS->>DDB: Query the account's feed after the cursor
  DDB-->>MS: the changes
  MS-->>Edge: changes and next_cursor
  Edge-->>Dev: changes and next_cursor
  Dev->>Edge: POST /blocks/urls, the version, the hashes it lacks
  Edge->>MS: HTTP
  MS->>DDB: GetItem, the version, and the share if not the caller's
  DDB-->>MS: the block list, the membership
  alt the hashes are in a version the caller may read
    MS-->>Edge: presigned GET URLs
    Edge-->>Dev: the URLs
    Dev->>S3: GET the block
    S3-->>Dev: the bytes
    Note over Dev: hash verified on read
  else not readable
    MS-->>Edge: 403
    Edge-->>Dev: 403
  end
blocks.legend: The device downloads only the block it does not have: the new version's block list is compared with the blocks already on the device. The metadata service signs a download URL only for hashes that belong to the version it just read, in an account the caller owns or a folder shared with the caller; the signature is the task role's and is valid until it expires s21. A block in Glacier Instant Retrieval is read the same way, with millisecond access s23; the neutral reassembly cost of the cold tier is S3's, not the client's.

blocks.text: Only the version check, the sequence read and this cursor fetch use strongly consistent reads; every other lookup can read eventually consistent data.
The background path: counting references, and removing blocks nobody points to.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 79 participant DDB as DynamoDB participant RC as Stream fn participant Sch as Scheduler participant GC as Sweep fn participant S3 as S3 Note over DDB: a version item is put, or
a superseded one expires by TTL DDB-)RC: stream record RC->>DDB: refcount +1 or -1 per block, once per version Note over RC,DDB: zero_since is set when a count is 0
and removed when it rises above 0 Sch-)GC: invoke, every hour GC->>DDB: Query the sparse index, zero_since older than two days DDB-->>GC: block hashes GC->>DDB: delete the item if refcount is still 0 GC->>S3: DeleteObject
blocks.legend: This is the neutral tiering and garbage-collection step, and none of it is on a request path. The tiering itself needs no worker: a lifecycle rule moves blocks to Glacier Instant Retrieval by age s25. For the references, a version item gets a TTL of 30 days only when a commit supersedes it (or when its file is deleted), never while it is current, and a TTL delete, which DynamoDB performs within a few days of the expiry time, reaches the stream as a service deletion s19; the stream function counts once per version with a marker item, so a retried record counts nothing twice. Only blocks with a zero count appear in the sparse index s16, and the sweep waits two days, longer than the 24 hours the stream keeps its records, so that neither a block uploaded but not yet committed nor a count still on its way through the stream can make it delete a block that a version references. The schedule is EventBridge Scheduler, and its execution role may invoke the sweep function s36.

blocks.text: The tiering has no worker here: the lifecycle rule runs inside S3. S3 does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB by default s48, so the rule carries a size filter that lets the small last block of a file move too. A block deleted from the cold class within 90 days of its move is still billed for those days, which the cost pillar row names.

blocks.caption: Identity and network: who may call what, over which endpoint, and what is public. Three entries are public: the load balancer (in public subnets), the WebSocket API and, for presigned URLs only, the S3 endpoint. Every ECS service runs in private subnets across three Availability Zones in awsvpc mode, one network interface per task, each service under its own IAM task role, so permissions go to the task and not to a host. A task in a private subnet pulls its image through the Amazon ECR interface endpoints and an S3 gateway endpoint, and this design uses those, not a NAT gateway.

Notification: WebSocket API, its authorizer and its function

the authorizer validates the device token and returns the account id; the function reads the stream; writes, queries and deletes in the connections table (it registers on $connect and removes on $disconnect); writes one transaction per member into the members' partitions of the metadata table; may post to connections of the API

blocks.caption: The block store: Amazon S3 with a lifecycle rule, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, or a storage fleet you run.

rows.option: Amazon S3 Standard, with a lifecycle rule to Glacier Instant Retrieval
rows.pick_when: objects are immutable, named by key and read whole, durability should not be your operation, and the age at which data turns cold is known
rows.avoid_when: the objects are so small and so many that request and per-object charges become the bill, or the scale is where a bespoke fleet beats S3's price
rows.example: For this design: chosen. A block is immutable and named by its hash, S3 stores it across at least three zones and repairs it, and a lifecycle rule moves it to the cold class by age; the neutral repair and tiering workers become S3 settings.

rows.pick_when: access patterns are unknown and the objects are large, so the automatic move by last access beats guessing an age
rows.avoid_when: the objects number in the billions: the monitoring fee is charged per object, about $0.0025 per 1,000 a month
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. At billions of blocks the monitoring fee alone would be at least about $156,000 a month, and a block's age is known, so a lifecycle rule does the job without the fee.

rows.option: A storage fleet you run on EC2, the Magic Pocket shape
rows.pick_when: the scale is large enough that building replication, erasure coding and repair pays for the team that runs them, as Dropbox's description of its own system argues
rows.avoid_when: the team would rebuild what S3 already does, with the on-call load of repairing disks
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. The hot and cold tiers and the repair and tiering workers of the neutral design are what S3 provides; a fleet is the question the 10x row raises at an exabyte, not a day-one choice.

blocks.caption: Getting a block into S3: presigned URLs, a proxy through the block service, or S3 multipart upload.

rows.option: A presigned PUT per block, signed by the block service
rows.pick_when: the client can reach S3, the bytes need no transformation, and the service should carry requests, not bytes
rows.avoid_when: the service must inspect or transform the bytes, or clients cannot reach S3 directly
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The peak ingest is 12 GB a second, which stays between the clients and S3; the block service only signs URLs and records blocks.

rows.option: A proxy through the block service
rows.pick_when: the service must scan, transform or meter the bytes, or clients can reach only your own domain
rows.avoid_when: the volume is high: every byte crosses a load balancer and a task, and the fleet is sized for traffic instead of requests
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing needs to read the bytes, and the hash check is S3's checksum on the upload.

rows.pick_when: one large object, around a hundred megabytes or more, is uploaded in parts of at least 5 MiB, each part retried alone
rows.avoid_when: each unit is smaller than a part: parts must be at least 5 MiB, except the last
rows.example: For this design: does not apply. A block is at most 4 MB, under the part minimum, so each block is one PutObject; the resumable unit is the block, and the file is a list of block hashes.

blocks.caption: The metadata store: DynamoDB or Aurora PostgreSQL.

rows.option: Amazon DynamoDB, on-demand, with the account id as the partition key
rows.pick_when: access is by key within one tenant, a commit is a handful of items that must succeed together, strongly consistent reads are needed, and the table must grow without resharding
rows.avoid_when: the hot path needs joins, ad hoc queries across accounts, or a single record larger than the item size limit
rows.example: For this design: chosen. Every item of an account shares one partition key, a commit is one transaction over five items, a version item carries its block list, and the shard assignment of the neutral design is DynamoDB's own.

rows.pick_when: the product needs relational queries over the namespace, such as search by name across accounts, reporting, or SQL tooling
rows.avoid_when: the load is key lookups and one small transaction per account, so sharding accounts over clusters becomes a router and a field you run
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. One cluster would hold years of this metadata, so size is not the reason; the router that assigns each account to a cluster, the neutral metadata_shard field, would be ours to build and run.

blocks.caption: The change feed and the notification: DynamoDB items with Streams and a WebSocket API, Kinesis, or long polling on ECS; SNS mobile push as an extension.

rows.option: Feed items in the metadata table, DynamoDB Streams to a Lambda function, an API Gateway WebSocket API
rows.pick_when: the feed must be queried by account and cursor and written in the commit's transaction, and a hint should reach an open connection without a fleet to route it
rows.avoid_when: hints must be guaranteed or ordered, or the stream must be replayed beyond its 24 hours
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The feed is an ordered sequence per account in the same transaction as the version, the stream only carries the hint, and API Gateway holds the connections, so no task has to be told which one to call.

rows.option: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams as the feed
rows.pick_when: many consumers read the same ordered records, or history must be replayed
rows.avoid_when: the reader asks for everything of one account after a cursor, atomically with a write elsewhere
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. A stream is read in shard order, not by account, and cannot be written in the commit's transaction, so the feed would still need a table.

rows.option: Long polling on ECS behind the load balancer
rows.pick_when: clients cannot use WebSockets, and the connected devices are few enough for a small fleet to hold; the idle timeout is raised from its default
rows.avoid_when: millions of devices stay connected: each change must reach the task that holds a device's connection, which needs a routing layer of its own
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. It is the neutral default and works at small scale, but the routing from a commit to the right task is what API Gateway's connection ids already give.

rows.option: Amazon SNS mobile push, the extension
rows.pick_when: the app is asleep on a phone and only the push service of the platform can wake it
rows.avoid_when: the device is a desktop that holds its own connection
rows.example: For this design: not part of this pass. A connected phone is already pushed to over the WebSocket; waking a sleeping app would add a platform endpoint per phone and a publish from the notification function, with the same hint as payload, and is not drawn here.

blocks.caption: The services and the stream functions: ECS on Fargate, Lambda or EKS.

rows.pick_when: steady, request-shaped services behind a load balancer, with no cluster to patch
rows.avoid_when: the load is bursty and mostly idle, or a Kubernetes estate already exists
rows.example: For this design: chosen for the metadata service, with its sharing routes, and the block service: steady request traffic, with a peak of 11,600 commits a second, on Arm tasks across three Availability Zones, scaled on request rate.

rows.pick_when: event-shaped work with uneven volume: one invocation per batch of stream records or per schedule tick
rows.avoid_when: steady, high-rate request traffic, where per-request billing exceeds the tasks
rows.example: For this design: chosen for the notification function, the stream function and the sweep, which react to stream records and a schedule; not for the request-path services.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes and needs its ecosystem
rows.avoid_when: three small services and no Kubernetes estate; the upgrade cadence buys nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing needs the Kubernetes API, and a cluster brings three major releases a year to track for three services.

blocks.caption: The design reviewed against the six Well-Architected pillars.
columns: what it asks of this design
rows: make frequent, small, reversible changes; anticipate failure; learn from operational events

alarms on the conflict rate, the stream's iterator age and the age of the oldest zero-count block; a scheduled restore test of the metadata table from its backups, because replication does not protect against a wrong delete
the reference counts are eventually consistent, so a counting bug leaks blocks, which costs money and loses nothing; finding a leak needs a reconciliation job that is not built here
a strong identity foundation; security at all layers; protect data in transit and at rest; keep people away from data

one IAM task role per service; blocks private in a bucket that accepts signed requests only; URLs that carry the block service's role and expire; HTTPS everywhere; download URLs signed only after the access check
a presigned URL works for anyone who holds it until it expires, so the expiry is kept short and the URL is never logged
automatically recover from failure; scale horizontally; stop guessing capacity
blocks across at least three zones in S3; one DynamoDB transaction per commit; ECS replacing failed tasks; every hint recoverable by the cursor fetch; a conflict becomes a copy, never an overwrite
a very busy account meets a partition's write limit until its namespace is split; a device offline for longer than the stream's 24 hours refetches by cursor from the table
consider mechanical sympathy; use serverless architectures where they fit
bytes go between the client and S3, not through a task; one PutObject per block, no multipart; strongly consistent reads only for the version check, the sequence read and the cursor fetch
a block read from the cold class costs more per request and per GB than one from Standard
adopt a consumption model; analyze and attribute expenditure

a lifecycle rule by age, not Intelligent-Tiering, whose fee is per object; the cold class's price per GB as the lever, since the 30-day Standard tail is a small share of the bytes; cost per logical TB per month by tier on the dashboard
a block deleted from Glacier Instant Retrieval within 90 days of moving there is still billed for the 90; age is not last access, so an old block read daily pays the retrieval fee
maximize utilization; use managed services; understand your impact
S3 pools the storage of every customer instead of a fleet of our own; cold blocks in the cold class; Lambda functions that run only on events; Arm Fargate tasks
the blocks of the last 30 days sit in Standard even if they are never read again, under one percent of the bytes

blocks.caption: What the picks cost at AWS list prices for US East (N. Virginia) as of 2026-10-16, at 730 hours a month, counting 1 TB as 1,000 GB as the neutral table does; the unit prices are read from the Price List Bulk API and prices change.

S3 PUT and one lifecycle transition per new block: 2.1 billion a month at 1 MB a block (assumption), the rule's size filter lowered so that blocks under 128 KB move too

DynamoDB on-demand: 3 billion commits a month at 10 write units, with the reference counting at 4 (one block a commit, assumption), 2.1 billion block puts, and per commit two strongly consistent reads (the node, the sequence) and a half-unit batch read
DynamoDB Standard: 36 TB after a year (the neutral 18 TB, doubled for the per-item overhead of a version, a feed item and a marker; assumption)
ECS on Fargate, 70 Arm tasks of 2 vCPU and 4 GB, sized for the peak (assumption); ten times the tasks at ten times the size

the five lines above; the load balancer, block reads and retrievals, change notification, the Lambda functions, the sharing and fan-out writes, the interface endpoints (ECR) and data transfer are not priced, because the exercise states no read rate, no connected devices and no members per share

blocks.text: Storage is more than nine tenths of the priced total at both sizes. Within it the cold class is about 96 percent of the storage bill and the Standard tail of the last 30 days about 4 percent, so the age in the lifecycle rule moves little: the cold class's price per GB and its 90-day minimum on deleted blocks are the levers. The list price of the cold class sits far below the neutral table's assumed price per raw disk.

blocks.text: Sharing endpoints change membership and write a change into every member's feed, which is how a shared folder stays eventually consistent across accounts without a transaction across shards.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: A user saves a modified 10 MB file on a laptop; the phone gets it. The step numbers run on across the four parts.

blocks.title: Chunk and hash, on the client
items: The client detects the change, splits the file into three 4 MB blocks (the last one smaller), hashes each, and compares with the previous version's block list: one block changed, so only one new hash. This is delta sync; the cost of a small edit is one block, not the file.

blocks.text: Part a: the first commit, which finds the one missing block.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber participant C as Client participant MS as Metadata service participant MD as Metadata DB participant BS as Block service C->>MS: commit, new block list,
parent version MS->>MD: check the parent version MD-->>MS: it matches Note over MS,MD: the optimistic check
that detects conflicts MS->>BS: which of these blocks exist? BS-->>MS: one is missing MS-->>C: 409, the one missing block
blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed. The commit names blocks by their hash, the unit Dropbox's Magic Pocket description uses s1.

blocks.text: Part b: the upload of the missing block, idempotent and resumable.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 7 participant C as Client participant BS as Block service participant HOT as Hot block store C->>BS: PUT the block, by its hash alt the block already exists BS-->>C: acknowledged, no transfer Note over C,BS: another user uploaded the same bytes:
this is the deduplication else a new block BS->>HOT: store, replicated HOT-->>BS: durable BS-->>C: 201 end Note over C,BS: an interrupted PUT is simply repeated
blocks.legend: The hash is the name, so repeating a PUT cannot create a second copy. The block is replicated before the block service acknowledges it.

blocks.text: Part c: the second commit writes the version, the node record and the change in one transaction.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 12 participant C as Client participant MS as Metadata service participant MD as Metadata DB participant N as Change feed C->>MS: commit again MS->>MD: new version and node record,
one transaction on the shard MD-->>MS: durable, replica in sync MS->>N: append a change to the account's feed MS-->>C: the version Note over C,MS: an acknowledged commit
means the file is durable
blocks.legend: Every block exists, so the commit now succeeds. The acknowledgement is safe because the blocks were replicated before their PUT was acknowledged and the metadata write is synchronously replicated.

blocks.text: Part d: the phone learns of the change and downloads only the block it lacks.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 17
  participant P as Phone
  participant NS as Notification service
  participant MS as Metadata service
  participant BS as Block service
  NS-)P: the long poll returns
  P->>MS: fetch changes after the cursor
  MS-->>P: the change list: a new version
  P->>BS: GET the one block it lacks
  BS-->>P: the block
blocks.legend: The open arrow at step 17 is a hint, not data: the cursor fetch at step 18 is what guarantees the phone sees every change once.

blocks.title: Later, in the background
items: Later, a tiering worker moves blocks not read for 30 days (assumption) into erasure-coded stripes; a garbage collector unreferences blocks whose versions passed the retention window and whose refcount is zero.

blocks.text: Bytes are the bottleneck, and they scale horizontally: block servers are added by capacity, and placement spreads a block's replicas or fragments across failure domains (disk, rack, zone). Repair is the subtle part: when a disk dies, every stripe or replica set it held must be rebuilt from the survivors before another failure in the same set, so the design states a repair time (hours, not days) and sizes repair bandwidth for it; durability is a function of failure rate and repair time, not of replica count alone.

blocks.caption: The durability schemes side by side.
rows: two simultaneous losses of a block's copies
the hot tier: recent and frequently read blocks
any 4 lost fragments of a stripe
the cold tier: blocks not read for 30 days

blocks.text: The SRE book's data integrity chapter adds the layer most designs forget: replication protects against hardware loss, not against a bug or an operator deleting the wrong thing, so soft deletion, backups of metadata and regular restore tests are part of the design, and the restore is the real test. The S3 write-up adds the operational detail that heat must be balanced across disks so that popular blocks do not sit on a few spindles.

Metadata is small but hot and must be consistent: 11,600 commits per second at peak across shards keyed by account, each a transaction on one shard, with no cross-shard transactions because a file belongs to one account's namespace; sharing is modelled as a membership record plus feed fan-out, not as a cross-shard write. The change feed per account is a log with a monotonic sequence, which makes the sync cursor simple: a device asks for everything after its cursor and is never told the same change twice. Notification is long poll by default and push on mobile; both are hints, since the cursor fetch is what guarantees completeness.
Each row names the failure, what the user sees, and the mitigation.

blocks.caption: Failure modes.
rows: no user-visible effect if repair is on time
replicas or fragments across failure domains; repair workers with a stated time budget; alert on under-replicated blocks
that account group cannot commit; downloads still work
synchronous replica promoted; clients retry commits with the same block list (idempotent by parent version)
blocks are idempotent PUTs by hash; the client resumes block by block
optimistic version check on commit (412); never silently overwrite
soft delete for 30 days; versions restorable; the delete is a metadata change, blocks remain

verify the hash on read and on repair; a mismatch quarantines the copy and re-reads another. A genuine SHA-256 collision (two different blocks with one hash) is outside the threat model: a hash check cannot detect it by definition, and the design rests on the collision resistance of the hash

the gap between the rows is the lifecycle policy's worth, which is why it becomes a platform concern

blocks.text: At this scale the storage is a platform, and the number the team is held to is the cost per logical TB per month by tier: every lifecycle, placement and repair decision moves it, and the restore test is still the only proof that the bytes are there.

L1: Chunked, content-addressed blocks in an object store, with a separate metadata service that owns files, versions and block lists.
A commit protocol that reports missing blocks and makes uploads idempotent and resumable.
The ingest and storage arithmetic from the stated assumptions (100 TB per day, 250 PB logical).
L2: Delta sync by block list diff, conflict detection by parent version with conflicted copies, and a cursor-driven change feed per account.
Deduplication by hash and what it saves; the durability arithmetic of replication versus erasure coding with a chosen code.
Repair time as part of durability, and failure-domain-aware placement.
Soft deletion, metadata backups and restore tests as defence in depth beyond replication.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: the storage unit, offline conflicts, namespace consistency, retention, hot versus cold, regions. Say the numbers aloud: 11,600 commits per second at peak, 100 TB ingested per day, 250 PB logical, 350 PB on disk with a 10-plus-4 code versus 750 PB replicated.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Node, Version with a block list, Block by hash, Share, Cursor and ChangeFeed; the commit, block PUT, changes and notify endpoints.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: clients that chunk and hash, the metadata service on account shards, the block service with hot and cold tiers, the change feed and notification path.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: the sync protocol (commit with missing blocks, idempotent block uploads, delta sync, version conflicts, the cursor), then durability (replication versus erasure coding arithmetic, placement, repair time, soft delete and restores).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan (lifecycle, geography, verification, namespace splits), and the L3 sentence: durability is a function of failure rate and repair time, and the restore test is the only proof.
Context and scope: The client platforms, the existing object store if any, the retention and sharing requirements, and the incident or cost that motivates the design.
Goals and non-goals: Never lose an acknowledged file, sync within 10 s, 30-day history, resumable uploads; no collaborative editing, no content search, no end-to-end encryption.
Design: This answer fills it: the block and metadata split, the commit protocol, the tiers, the change feed.
Alternatives considered: Whole-file storage, replication everywhere, an eventually consistent namespace, last-writer-wins conflicts, timer polling, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Security (per-account authorization on every node, sharing roles, encryption at rest), privacy (hash-based dedupe across accounts and what it reveals), observability (under-replicated blocks, repair backlog, commit latency, sync lag per device), cost per TB per month by tier, rollout by account cohort with the old store as fallback.
Review questions the doc must answer: How long a block may be under-replicated after a disk failure and what bandwidth repair needs, and what two devices see after editing the same file offline.
